stories.headline: Is stubble burning in Punjab affecting Sri Lanka’s air quality?
stories.deck: Pollution from northern India and the wider region travels over the Bay of Bengal to Sri Lanka during the northeast monsoon, and crop burning is part of that mix
stories.bodyText:
In the months of October and November, farmers in Punjab and Haryana burn leftover rice stalks to clear their fields for wheat. The smoke chokes Delhi, but it does not stay there.
In mid-November 2026, Sri Lanka’s Central Environmental Authority reported raised levels of fine dust (PM2.5 and PM10) across the Northern Province and in Anuradhapura, Puttalam, Trincomalee, Kurunegala and Colombo. It blamed much of this on winds blowing in from outside the island.

stories.headline: Putin commissions nuclear submarine carrying hypersonic missiles
stories.deck: Russian President Vladimir Putin oversaw the commissioning of a new nuclear-powered submarine called the Perm. This submarine is notable for being equipped with Russian-made Zircon hypersonic missiles. Putin stated that the navy will receive five additional submarines by 2030, enhancing its capabilities. The Perm is a fourth-generation submarine in the Yasen-M class designed for covert underwater…
stories.bodyText:
Russian President Vladimir Putin on Friday commissioned a new nuclear-powered submarine, which Moscow claims is the first in its fleet equipped with Russian-made Zircon hypersonic missiles.
The Perm will be followed by planned induction of five more nuclear-powered submarines into Russian navy by 2030, AFP reported.
Putin attended the flag-raising ceremony of the submarine at the Sevmash shipyard in Severodvinsk, in northwestern Russia, marking its formal transfer to the navy, according to a video released by the Kremlin.
“Russia is one of the few countries in the world capable of building powerful nuclear submarines of this kind, weapons with global reach and significance,” Putin said.
Nuclear-powered submarines form a key component of Russia's nuclear deterrence, as their ability to operate covertly underwater provides the country with a second-strike capability in the event of a nuclear attack.
Putin said the navy would receive five additional submarines by 2030, including three Yasen-M class vessels, the same class as the Perm. He said the submarines could operate in “any part of the world’s oceans” while carrying various cruise missiles.
Putin also reiterated Moscow's commitment to modernising its navy, expressing confidence that plans to build a powerful naval force would be implemented fully and on schedule.
The Perm is a fourth-generation nuclear-powered attack submarine of the Russian Navy and the sixth vessel in the Project 885 series,built under the upgraded Project 885M (08851), also known as the Yasen-M class.
It is the second Russian submarine to be named after the city of Perm, with the predecessor being the B-292 Perm, a Project 671RTMK vessel.

stories.headline: Karunadotsava | List of prominent companies founded by Kannadigas
stories.bodyText:
An illuminated Vidhana Soudha
Credit: DH File Photo
This year, Karnataka is celebrating the 70th anniversary of its formation. It was formed as Mysore State on November 1, 1956, and renamed Karnataka on the same date in 1973.
While Bengaluru has rightfully earned its reputation as India's technology and startup capital, the State's business legacy is equally reflected in companies founded by Kannadigas outside the metropolis.
As Karnataka marks a historic milestone, here is a look at some iconic legacy businesses whose origins are deeply rooted in the Karunadu and whose reach extends well beyond its borders.
Infosys founders N R Narayana Murthy (centre) with Nandan Nilekani, Kris Gopalakrishna (R), K Dinesh and Srinath Batni (L).
Credit: PTI File Photo
Infosys Ltd was founded in 1981 by seven engineers: N R Narayana Murthy, Nandan Nilekani, S Gopalakrishnan, S D Shibulal, K Dinesh, N S Raghavan and Ashok Arora.
Narayana Murthy and his colleagues started the business with an initial capital of just Rs 10,000, reportedly supported by his wife, Sudha Murty. Though it was first set up in Pune, the company moved its headquarters to Bengaluru and built its brand reputation on software exports, professional management and the global delivery model. Its growth helped establish Bengaluru as a major global technology hub.
Today, Infosys is among India's largest IT services exporters, offering consulting, cloud, artificial intelligence, engineering and digital transformation services.
Employee strength: Approximately 3.29 lakh.
Approximate clients (national and international): Included in 1,965 active clients in around 59 countries.
Biocon Ltd executive chairperson Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw
Credit: Reuters Photo
It was established on November 29, 1978, by Kiran Mazumdar-Shaw. She began operations in the garage of a rented house at Koramangala, a suburb of Bengaluru.
A trained brewer, she initially faced considerable challenges entering the biotechnology industry, which was then relatively unfamiliar in India. Her determination to build a science-led Indian enterprise eventually transformed Biocon into a major biotechnology company.
In partnership with Ireland-based Biocon Biochemicals, it has grown to become a global powerhouse in the biotechnology industry.
Today, Biocon operates in biopharmaceuticals, biosimilars, generics and research-based healthcare solutions. Its products serve patients and healthcare systems across international markets.
Employee strength: Around 16,500 worldwide
Global presence: Around 120 nations
Manipal Hospitals in Bengaluru.
Credit: DH Photo/S K Dinesh
The Manipal Group traces its origins to Dr T M A Pai (Tonse Madhava Ananth Pai ), who established several pioneering institutions in Karnataka.
A doctor by profession, his entrepreneurial journey began with banking and community development before moving into education and healthcare. In 1953, T M A Pai founded Kasturba Medical College in Manipal, operating as a public-private collaboration with government hospitals in Mangaluru.
For his outstanding contribution to society, T M A Pai was awarded the Padma Shri by the Government of India in 1972.
His son Ramdas Pai subsequently expanded the institution's academic reach, strengthened its university structure and helped establish Manipal as a recognised international education and healthcare brand.
The first branch of Manipal Hospitals was established on HAL Airport Road, Bengaluru, in 1991.
For his philanthropic works, Ramdas Pai was awarded the Padma Bhushan in 2011.
Today, the wider Manipal ecosystem includes education, healthcare, research and other business interests. Manipal Hospitals alone has grown into a major healthcare network.
It should be noted that Ramdas Pai's son Ranjan Pai, a medical doctor by qualification, also runs his own businesses, including educational institutions and hospitals. Ranjan Pai is the founder and chairman of the Manipal Education and Medical Group, which runs seven universities and 29 hospitals across the globe.
VRL Group chairman Vijay Sankeshwar
Vijayanand Roadlines Ltd (VRL) Group was founded in 1976 by Vijay Sankeshwar in Gadag, Karnataka. His entrepreneurial journey began with a single truck and a vision to build a dependable goods transportation business.
Over the years, it gradually expanded into Bengaluru, Hubballi and Belagavi before developing a nationwide transportation network.
Now, VRL has diversified into parcel transportation, courier services, priority cargo, passenger transportation and logistics solutions.
Employee strength: 20,000-plus with approximately
National reach: 1,249-plus goods transport branches and franchise locations with 5,745 owned goods transport vehicles.
Narayana Health chairman Devi Shetty
Credit: PTI Photo
Narayana Health (previously known as Narayana Hrudyalaya) was founded by Devi Prasad Shetty, a legendary cardiac surgeon. The core theme of the organisation was to make high-quality healthcare accessible to common citizens of the country.
After gaining medical experience in India and the United Kingdom, he returned to India and became known for his work in cardiac surgery. In 2000, he established Narayana Hrudayalaya in Bengaluru. The organisation subsequently expanded into a multispecialty healthcare network and adopted the Narayana Health brand in 2013.
Narayana Health operates hospitals, heart centres, clinics and other healthcare facilities. Its services cover cardiac care, cancer treatment, neurology, orthopaedics, renal sciences and other specialities. It operates across 11 Indian cities, including Bengaluru, and has two hospitals in the Cayman Islands.
Employee strength: Approximately 21,150
Utham Gowda
Credit: LinkedIn
Captain Fresh was founded by Utham Gowda, a first-generation entrepreneur from Mysuru who identified an opportunity to modernise India's fragmented seafood supply chain. Traditionally, seafood procurement involved multiple intermediaries, inconsistent quality standards, limited traceability and complex international distribution.
Gowda saw the potential to use technology, supply-chain integration and branded seafood products to connect fishermen, suppliers, processors, distributors and retailers. With an aim to develop a technology-driven seafood platform, he established Captain Fresh that could compete in international markets.
Captain Fresh has expanded beyond the Indian market through acquisitions, international sourcing and branded seafood distribution.
Its portfolio includes brands such as CenSea, Koral, Senecrus, ChopServe and Ocean Garden.
During FY2025, the company reported serving 1,291 customers across 34 countries, with a sourcing network of 659 suppliers across 35 countries.
As per the company's LinkedIn profile, it has 200-500 employees with 405 associated members.
Zerodha co-founders Nithin Kamath (L) and Nikhil Kamath.
Zerodha Broking Ltd was founded by brothers Nithin Kamath and Nikhil Kamath as a discount brokerage firm in August 2010.
The company's name has a very interesting meaning: it is a mix of 'zero' and 'rodha', the Sanskrit word for barrier. A barrier-free platform for people to make retail trading of stocks, derivatives, currencies, commodities, mutual funds, and bonds.
The company started with six employees and Rs 2 crore in seed money drawn from Nithin Kamath's personal savings and contributions from a Singapore-based friend.
By mid-2020, it became a unicorn with a one-billion-dollar valuation and has more than 13 lakh customers. The subscriber base soon rose to one crore by the end of 2022. Currently, it has over 1,200 employees and is valued at more than $3.5 billion.
Coffee Day Enterprises founder V G Siddhartha
Cafe Coffee Day was founded by V G Siddhartha, an entrepreneur from Chikkamagaluru who came from a family associated with coffee cultivation. He studied economics and initially worked in the financial markets before entering the coffee business.
In the early 1990s, he began building a coffee procurement and trading business, subsequently expanding into coffee plantations and retail.
In 1996, he opened the first Cafe Coffee Day outlet on Brigade Road in Bengaluru. His aim was to create a welcoming social space where young Indians could meet, work and enjoy affordable coffee.
Cafe Coffee Day became one of India's pioneering organised café chains, helping popularise the café culture among students, professionals and urban consumers. Its business evolved to include cafés, coffee vending machines, packaged coffee and other retail offerings. Its historical success was built around a large domestic store network and a recognisable Indian coffee brand.
Following Siddhartha's death in 2019, his wife, Malavika Hegde, took over the reins.
After years of losses and store closures, the company reported its first annual profit since 2019-20 in FY26. It registered net profit of Rs 28 crore on Rs 269 crore in revenue in Q1 FY-26.
Shashi Kumar, co-founder and CEO, Akshayakalpa Farms and Foods Pvt Ltd, at a cow shed on his farm near Tiptur in Tumakuru district.
Akshayakalpa Organic was co-founded by Shashi Kumar and G N S Reddy in 2010.
Shashi Kumar's entrepreneurial journey is particularly interesting because he moved from a successful technology career into agriculture.
After completing his engineering education and spending approximately 17 years in the technology sector, including 13 years at Wipro, he became interested in the structural challenges faced by Indian farmers. He recognised that small dairy farmers needed better incomes, scientific farming support and a dependable route to market. The company was established to develop a farmer-led organic dairy model that could improve rural livelihoods while supplying consumers with quality organic food.
Akshayakalpa works with farmers to develop sustainable dairy operations through training, animal care, organic farming practices and direct procurement systems. Its product portfolio includes milk, curd, paneer, ghee, butter and other dairy products.
As per reports, Akshayakalpa Organic's network has around 2,800 farmers across Karnataka, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh.
Rohith Bhat, founder of Robosoft Technologies and 99Games.
Robosoft Technologies was founded in 1996 by Rohith Bhat in Udupi, Karnataka. His entrepreneurial journey began when he identified an opportunity in software development for Apple Macintosh computers. At a time when India's software industry was largely focused on outsourced IT services, Bhat wanted to build a company specialising in digital products and user experiences.
Starting with a small team, Robosoft gradually expanded its capabilities into mobile applications, user experience design and enterprise technology In 2022, the company was acquired by Japan's TechnoPro Group for around Rs 805 crore.
Also, it should be noted that Rohith Bhat founded 99Games in Udupi, in 2008.
The company emerged during the early growth of Apple's App Store, when smartphones were beginning to create new opportunities for independent game developers.
Just like Rajesh Rao, who pioneered game development with Dhruva Interactive (which later acquired by Grand Theft Auto-maker Rockstar Games) in Bengaluru, Rohith Bhat recognised that Indian developers could create games for international audiences rather than simply developing software for outsourcing clients.
99Games began with a small team of developers and launched its early games, including chess titles, on Apple's App Store. Its early success demonstrated that a technology company from a small Karnataka city could stand out in the global mobile gaming industry.
99Games is credited to development of mobile games, casual entertainment products and original gaming intellectual property. Some prominent titles include Dhoom:3 The Game and Star Chef.
There are many more companies worth mentioning, including Air Deccan (founded by Capt G R Gopinath), and new and upcoming firms such as Wellbi (by Supreeth Kashyap), Xpheno (by Kamal Karanth), The Good Doll (by Suhas Ramegowda), Bounce Infinity (Vivekananda Hallekere), Real Fast AI (by Sidu Ponnappa), Sonic Lamb ( by Navajith Karkera), and Cuzor Labs (by Sachin Naik) that inspire thousands of new generation of Kannadigas to take up the enterprenuership with confidence and bring laurels to Karnataka.

stories.headline: 131st vs 132nd Amendment Bills: What has changed in the Centre's delimitation proposal
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Centre is set to introduce the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, in the Lok Sabha on Monday, seeking to implement one-third reservation for women in Parliament and state and Union territory legislative assemblies through a fresh delimitation exercise.
The proposed legislation differs from the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, defeated in the Lok Sabha in April, mainly in its approach to delimitation, the allocation of seats among states and the census data to be used for redrawing constituencies.
Here are the key differences between the two proposals:Uniform 50 per cent increase in seats for all states and UTs
The most significant change in the 132nd Amendment Bill is the provision for a uniform 50 per cent increase in the number of seats in the Lok Sabha and the legislative assemblies of every state and Union territory.
The fresh Bill proposes to increase the Lok Sabha's maximum strength to 850, comprising up to 815 members from states and 35 from Union territories. It also seeks to raise the ceiling on the strength of state assemblies from 500 to 650.
The earlier 131st Amendment Bill did not provide for a uniform percentage increase in seats across states. Under the fresh proposal, applying the same 50 per cent increase to each state's existing strength would broadly preserve its share of seats in the Lok Sabha.
Use of 2011 Census figures for delimitation
The two proposals also differ in the census data they allow for delimitation.
The 2023 women's reservation law linked the implementation of the quota to delimitation after the publication of figures from the first census conducted after the law came into force.
The fresh Bill, however, allows constituency boundaries to be redrawn using the "latest published census figures available on the date of the commencement" of the proposed amendment. This effectively means the 2011 Census figures.
Revised seat allocations and boundaries to remain until 2051
The 132nd Amendment Bill proposes that the revised allocation of seats and the division of constituencies following delimitation remain in force until 2051.
The fresh proposal also provides for one-third reservation for women, including those belonging to the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, for 15 years from the commencement of the 2023 amendment. Parliament would have the power to extend the reservation period by law.
It would also determine the authority and manner in which seats reserved for women are rotated.
New Delimitation Commission to oversee the exercise
The accompanying Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026, provides for a three-member commission headed by a serving or former Supreme Court judge appointed by the Centre.

The commission would determine the allocation of seats, redraw constituencies and identify seats to be reserved for women.
Under the Bill, reserved seats would be allotted by rotation "as the Commission may deem fit". Seats reserved for women from the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes would be rotated within constituencies reserved for their respective categories.
Earlier Bill defeated in Lok Sabha in April
The earlier Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill was defeated in the Lok Sabha on April 17, falling short of the required two-thirds majority. A total of 298 MPs voted in favour of the Bill, while 230 voted against it.
The government subsequently did not proceed with the accompanying Bills.

briefs.headline: Gutkha worth ₹66.78 lakh seized from container in Thane’s Kalwa; driver arrested, seven others wanted
briefs.deck: Police seized 19,080 packets of banned gutkha concealed behind fans and hardware materials; total seizure valued at ₹94.78 lakh
briefs.bodyText:
The Kalwa police on Thursday (November 26, 2026) arrested a 32-year-old container driver for allegedly transporting banned gutkha worth ₹66.78 lakh after intercepting a vehicle near Parsik Circle in Kalwa. The police seized the gutkha along with the container, collectively valued at ₹94.78 lakh, and launched a search for seven other accused allegedly involved in the illegal transportation and distribution of the banned product.
According to the police, the operation was carried out at around 1:40 p.m. on November 26 after a team intercepted a suspicious Eicher container bearing registration number TG-12-U-1611 opposite Amit Garden on the Mumbra-Bhiwandi carriageway.
During the inspection, police found that fans, hardware materials, and other goods had allegedly been used to conceal the consignment and evade detection. A thorough search of the vehicle led to the recovery of 19,080 packets of banned ‘Gold 9000’ gutkha packed in 53 large sacks.
The seized gutkha was valued at ₹66.78 lakh, while the container was worth ₹28 lakh.
The arrested accused has been identified as Mehraj Karim Shaikh, 32, a resident of Bhiwandi and a native of Hyderabad.
Based on a complaint lodged by Food Safety Officer Aruna Veerkayade, the Kalwa police registered an FIR under relevant provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023.
Police are searching for seven other accused, including those allegedly involved in the manufacture, transportation and distribution of the banned gutkha. Investigators are also looking into the source of the consignment and its intended destination.
The seizure could potentially help uncover a larger gutkha smuggling and distribution network, with investigators probing the alleged involvement of manufacturers, transporters and distributors.
Assistant Police Inspector Santosh Pimple of the Kalwa police station is conducting further investigations.

briefs.headline: Study calls for uniform national framework to regulate ASHAs’ pay, roles
briefs.deck: Researchers flag widening gap between workers’ volunteer status and expanding responsibilities; seek better remuneration, workload limits and grievance redressal
briefs.bodyText:
While Accredited Social Health Activists (ASHAs) are on a prolonged strike in Karnataka, a recent study by researchers from the ICMR-National Institute for Vector Control Research, Puducherry, has called for a uniform national framework to ensure fair remuneration, clearly defined responsibilities and consistent benefits for workers across States.
It flags a growing contradiction in the programme: while ASHAs continue to be classified as volunteers, their responsibilities have expanded considerably, with many duties becoming increasingly structured and institutionalised.
The study, authored by Anoop C. Choolayil, Thamizhmaran Sundararajan and Vijesh Sreedhar Kuttiatt from the Institute, was published in BMJ Global Health last month. Titled ‘ASHA workers at the crossroads: navigating volunteerism and formalisation in the changing public health landscape’, it argues that inadequate and inconsistent remuneration, undefined roles, rising workloads and the absence of formal job security threaten the sustainability of the programme.
From community mobilisation to wider health duties
Launched in 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission, the ASHA programme is the world’s largest public-sector community health worker initiative, with nearly a million trained workers. ASHAs act as a link between communities and the healthcare system, particularly in underserved areas, and have played a significant role in promoting maternal and child health and improving access to essential services.
Initially, their work was envisaged as voluntary and limited to a few hours on four days a week, with a focus on health awareness, immunisation, antenatal care and institutional deliveries. They were paid incentives for completing specified tasks rather than a regular salary.
Over the years, however, their responsibilities have widened to include family planning, tuberculosis surveillance, health surveys, non-communicable disease screening, mental health awareness and digital data entry. During the COVID-19 pandemic, they were also assigned contact tracing, vaccination drives, surveillance and data management.
The researchers describe this transition as “informal formalisation” — a situation in which workers are increasingly bound by institutional protocols and reporting requirements without receiving the recognition, remuneration or security associated with formal employment.
Protests point to systemic gaps
To examine the demands of ASHAs, the researchers reviewed media reports on protests between January 2015 and March 2025. They screened around 800 search results and identified 30 distinct protest records for analysis.
The study points out that workers’ demands over the years have included better and timely remuneration, higher fixed honorariums, social security, health insurance, pension benefits, job security and recognition of their work. Although some protests have resulted in modest increases in honorariums and insurance coverage in certain cases, these measures have not addressed the structural problems, it says.
The fragmented system of incentive payments is another concern. Payments are linked to different activities and draw on separate funding pools, often resulting in delays. The absence of a single budget for remuneration to ASHAs adds to uncertainty, while additional duties assigned beyond their prescribed roles increase the workload.
WHO guidelines and proposed reforms
The researchers recommend a uniform national policy framework that provides a guaranteed base honorarium supplemented by task-based incentives. They call for written agreements setting out responsibilities and working conditions, streamlined payment systems and dedicated funding.
They also advocate workload assessments, clear limits on duties and accessible grievance redressal mechanisms through which workers can report the assignment of unauthorised tasks without fear of retaliation. A semi-formalised status under the National Health Mission, with greater recognition and clearer career progression pathways, could help address the gap between their official designation and actual work, the study suggests.
The recommendations draw on the WHO’s 2018 guidelines for community health workers, which emphasise on appropriate remuneration, clear contracting arrangements and supportive supervision.
The researchers acknowledge that implementing these reforms would require sustained political commitment and long-term financing. They point to fragmented funding and differences in governance and resource allocation across States as barriers to a common framework.

briefs.headline: Supreme Court orders Karthigai Deepam to be lit at ‘deepathoon’ on November 28; issues contempt notice
briefs.deck: Bench directs Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary, DGP, Madurai District Collector, temple authorities to be present for next hearing on Dec. 15; court sees ‘pre-meditated conspiracy' between State and temple trustees
briefs.bodyText:
Rejecting the Tamil Nadu government’s claim that it stayed aloof from the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy Temple management’s customary decisions, the Supreme Court on Friday (November 27, 2026) said non-compliance with its November 20 order to light the Karthigai Deepam on the deepathoon (stone pillar) atop the Thirupparankundram hill in Madurai amounted to “wilful disobedience” born of a “pre-meditated conspiracy” between the State and the temple trustees.
A Bench of Justices Aravind Kumar and Vipul M. Pancholi ordered the Board of Trustees of the temple to be suspended before appointing two former High Court judges – former Chief Justice of Meghalaya High Court S. Vaidyanathan and former Madras High Court judge Justice V. Parthiban - to act as Receivers.
The court directed the Karthigai Deepam to be lit again on Saturday (November 28, 2026), this time on the stone pillar, as was originally ordered on November 20. Central forces would provide security. The Receivers have to ensure the ceremony is carried out in consultation with the temple stanikars.
However, the interim order would not grant any future equities in favour of any party. The court made clear that its order was limited only to contempt petitions. The main case on religious rights concerning the Thirupparankundram lamp-lighting row would be heard in the second week of January 2027.
The row stems from the claims of ownership over the hilltop. The deepathoon is located near the Sikandar Badusha Dargah on top of the hill, while the Arulmigu Subramaniaswamy temple is at the base of the hill. The dargah side has claimed ownership of the hilltop, including the deepathoon site.
The court order comes two days after the ceremonial lamp was lit at the customary location – Deepa Mandapam – atop the hill and not as the Bench mandated.
Central security cover
In its order, the court allowed members of the public to light lamps on the Thirupparankundram hill on November 28. A 50-metre boundary around the dargah would be cordoned off. Access and rights of worshippers to the dargah would not be affected, the court ordered.
For the deepathoon ritual, authorities could either take the flame from the Deepa Mandapam or light one afresh, the court said.
The Bench issued show cause notices to the Tamil Nadu Chief Secretary, the State’s Director General of Police, Madurai District Collector and Police Commissioner, Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Commissioner and Deputy Commissioner, the chairperson, Executive Officer and trustees of the Subramaniswamy temple to respond as to why contempt action should not be issued against them for “brazen, calculated, mutual” disobedience of the November 20 order of the Supreme Court. The court ordered them to be personally present on December 15, the next date of hearing.
Call details sought
The Chief Secretary was directed to forthwith, and not later than 10 days, to file a personal affidavit explaining the “apparent disregard” shown by the State in performing its constitutional duty under Article 144 to obey a Supreme Court order. He was directed to provide details of the traffic of communication, including emails, call records, etc., between the State and district administration. One of the contempt petitioners had sought an inquiry into whether Government Ministers, including Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay, had a role to play in what happened on November 24.
“No person, however high, can defy a Supreme Court order. Anybody who tries to do that creates constitutional chaos. We will set this right… We will deal this with an iron hand,” Justice Kumar observed.
The Bench said its order was not an “invitation for negotiation”. If there was any modification to be done, the court would do it. Justice Kumar said temple trustees and the State authorities cannot read discretion or leeways into a Supreme Court order.
The Bench said ‘justice’ was a Preambular value. The stream of justice cannot be polluted by defying a Supreme Court directive. Any attempt to do so would not be tolerated.
Interpreting Supreme Court orders in silos or diluting them would amount to questioning the authority of the Supreme Court. Compliance instilled public confidence in the authority of the Supreme Court to administer justice, the Bench noted.
“When this court speaks, it speaks with the authority of the Constitution. It has to be obeyed. The Executive authorities have wilfully disobeyed. This strikes at the very root of law. It has to be dealt with iron hands,” the court observed.
The court said the District Collector was shedding “crocodile tears” with his version in a preliminary report that temple trustees refused to authorise a lamp-lighting team, and finally, lit the lamp at the “traditional” deepa mandapam.
Senior advocates A.M. Singhvi, Jaideep Gupta, Gopal Sankaranarayanan, Sidharth Luthra, and Additional Advocate General Prashanto Chandra Sen, appeared for the various State authorities.
Petitioners’ stance
The contempt petitioners termed the temple trustees as “stooges” of their political bosses in the State. They said these trustees did not have the “guts” to defy a Supreme Court order on their own and pass a resolution to light the lamp at the Deepa Mandapam rather than the stone pillar. They submitted that the Collector’s claim that he did “everything under the sun to ensure compliance with the November 20 order” was bogus.
“The State had already decided not to comply. The Board of trustees of the temple was chosen as the vehicle and refuge to hide behind. It was the weakest link in the administrative and political chain to justify this action… The Collector’s report was a tell-tale passing of the buck… He is just taking umbrage at the resolution of the devasthanam,” senior advocate Guru Krishnakumar submitted. He was joined in by senior advocates P. Valliappan and J. Saideepak Iyer.
Solicitor-General Tushar Mehta, for the Archaeological Survey of India, suggested a neutral agency to manage the temple.
The court said the contempt petitioners’ arguments and the State's responses invoked a sense of pain and anguish. It summarised the feeling in one word, “alas”.
Justice Kumar said it was hard to believe the Collector could not have done anything with the kind of powers he wielded within the district. The court expressed dissatisfaction with his report.
The Bench said the facts prima facie show a serious infraction on the part of the temple trustees, aided by State authorities, which has undermined the authority of the court. “This has shocked the conscience of the court,” Justice Kumar said.

briefs.headline: NCP-SP announces support to delimitation, Congress calls it ‘unfortunate’
briefs.deck: NCP-SP leader Jitendra Awhad said that while the party decided to support the Centre’s move, which has been opposed by the INDIA bloc, it would attend the bloc’s meeting on November 28
briefs.bodyText:
The Nationalist Congress Party–Sharadchandra Pawar (NCP-SP) on Friday (November 27, 2026) announced its support for the delimitation Bills.
The NCP-SP, led by Sharad Pawar and his daughter Supriya Sule, is a part of the Opposition bloc, the Indian National Developmental, Inclusive Alliance (INDIA). Most of the INDIA parties oppose the Centre’s delimitation plan, and the Congress has termed the decision of its ally, the NCP-SP, to support the Bills as "unfortunate". Earlier in the day, Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Sanjay Raut had referred to parties supporting the Bills as "traitors”.
NCP-SP leader Jitendra Awhad on Friday (November 27, 2026) said in Mumbai, “We will support the delimitation Bill. We will attend the INDIA Bloc meeting.” He was referring to a meeting of INDIA bloc floor leaders called for Saturday morning to discuss the Opposition’s joint response to the Bills.
Meanwhile, Ms. Sule will be in Mumbai over the weekend, as Mr. Pawar continues to remain hospitalised in the city. She will go to Delhi only on Monday (November 30) to attend the parliamentary session, she announced on her WhatsApp status. Mr. Pawar is likely to be discharged over the weekend, Mr. Awhad said.
“Supriya Sule, along with the eight party MPs, has decided to support the delimitation Bill. The party will do so accordingly. That is the final decision,” Mr. Awhad said minutes after meeting Mr. Pawar at hospital. The party has already issued a whip to all its leaders to remain present in Delhi.
When asked about his discussion with Mr. Pawar, he said that they did not discuss the party’s official stance per se. “The general point being discussed was that delimitation is a constitutional process. It will have to be done at some point,” he said.
The Union Cabinet on Friday approved the Constitution Amendment Bill, providing a proportionate increase of 50% seats across all States. This ratio will continue for 25 years till it changes in accordance with the population in the Census after 2051. The Women’s Reservation law will come into effect along with the increase in seats.
‘Deeply unfortunate’
Reacting to NCP SP’s announcement, Congress leader Sachin Sawant called the decision “deeply unfortunate”.
“It helps the [Narendra] Modi government’s authoritarian mindset. This Bill has been introduced to tighten the noose of authoritarianism that has been tightening for the past 12 years. The government’s intentions behind this Bill are not honest,” he said in a post on X.
However, Maharashtra Congress sources told The Hindu that the party had anticipated that the NCP-SP would take this stance.
The INDIA bloc has been rallying against the delimitation Bills. Criticising the Union government, Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut called the move a ploy. “Realising they are set to lose in 2029, they have devised a new ploy. They intend to bring in 860 MPs and carry out a delimitation exercise. This Bill is anti-national and anti-democratic; it must be opposed. Those who vote in favour of this Bill will be traitors to the nation. Their names will be recorded in history as traitors,” he said.
He added that the parties of the INDIA bloc cannot take an independent decision. “Whatever decision is to be taken will be taken within the INDIA bloc,” he said

briefs.headline: Bombay High Court gives go-ahead for Tata Sons board meeting on November 30
briefs.deck: The High Court says any outcome of the meeting would be subject to its final orders, declines any urgent relief on pleas challenging Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as executive chairman
briefs.bodyText:
The Bombay High Court on Friday (November 27, 2026) refused urgent relief to two Tata Trusts challenging the casting voting rights of reappointed executive chairman N. Chandrasekaran, ruling that Tata Sons' November 30 board meeting can proceed as scheduled, subject to the High Court's final orders.
A Bench of Justice Abhay Ahuja said it was not granting any immediate relief and that the meeting can go on as scheduled, but the same would be subject to the final orders of the court.
The Tata Trusts had sought for the meeting to be deferred or stayed or for an order that Mr. Chandrasekaran would not be allowed to exercise his vote as executive chairman.
During the hearing, the court asked what was the need to defer the meeting or not permit Mr. Chandrasekaran to cast his vote as executive chairman when he is already holding the post in his second term.
"We are not granting any relief today. Let the meeting (on November 30) go on as per schedule. Any outcome of the meeting would be subject to our final orders," the court said.
The Bench ordered Tata Sons and the other respondents in the case, which include the board members, to submit their reply affidavits to two suits filed on Thursday (November 26) and posted the matter for further hearing on January 18, 2027.
The Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and the RD Tata Trust (RDTT) had filed the suits in the High Court against Tata Sons and six of its directors, challenging the reappointment of Mr. Chandrasekaran as executive chairman for a third five-year term.
The SDTT has sought ₹50 crore, while the RDTT has demanded ₹15 crore in damages, with 18% annual interest, from Tata Sons.
As per the suits, the September 17 Tata Sons board resolution reappointing Chandrasekaran was invalid because it did not receive the affirmative vote required under Article 121 of the company's Articles of Association (AoA).
The immediate relief sought was to prevent the chairman of Tata Sons from exercising his casting vote during the November 30 board sitting in the event of a split in opinion among nominee directors.
On Friday (November 27, 2026), the Trusts' counsels also sought for the meeting to be deferred, which was opposed by Tata Sons.
"His (Chandrasekaran) third term is not coming into effect on Monday (November 30), right? He is already the chairman executive now. What are the plaintiffs (trusts) anticipating to happen during the November 30 meeting?" Justice Ahuja asked, seeking to know what was the need to defer the meeting or not permit Chandrasekaran to cast his vote.
There may be some other items on the agenda for the November 30 meeting other than confirmation of the reappointment of Mr. Chandrasekaran as executive chairman, the court said, adding those matters can be heard and decided.
Senior counsel Harish Salve, appearing for Tata Sons, said the board meeting needs to be held as it has got direction from the Reserve Bank of India giving a deadline of December 12 to inform the RBI of its (Tata Sons) decision (to comply with the mandated listing).
Any resolution passed would be subject to the orders of the High Court, Mr. Salve said.
Senior counsel Abhishek Manu Singhvi, appearing for the SDTT, said the RBI directive is just a ploy used by Tata Sons to show fake urgency to hold the meeting.
Mr. Singhvi sought a deferment of the board sitting on November 30, claiming that it has been called to confirm the minutes of the September 17 meeting during which it was decided to reappoint Mr. Chandrasekaran.
He pointed out Article 121 of the Articles of Association, which says such a decision cannot be taken unless there is an affirmative vote of the majority of the trustees.
When Noel Tata, who chairs Tata Trusts, had not given an affirmative voting in the September 17 meeting, then there was no majority and hence the next step of taking the vote of the other four board members could not have been initiated, Mr. Singhvi argued.
"Majority between two votes cannot be one vote. It has to be more than one. Noel Tata made it clear on September 17 that there was no affirmative majority vote. When Noel Tata disagreed there was lack of majority vote," Mr. Singhvi said.
The senior counsel added that Mr. Chandrasekaran's third term would be effective from February 27, 2027.
Mr. Singhvi submitted to the court the agenda of the November 30 meeting after which Justice Ahuja noted that one of the items was to confirm Chandrasekaran's reappointment.
Senior counsel Aspi Chinoy, appearing for RDTT, argued that the casting vote confirming the reappointment could not have been cast when there was no affirmative majority vote.
"The (reappointment) decision is perverse. They have destroyed the structure of the Articles that has governed the company for generations," he submitted.
Mr. Salve, appearing for Tata Sons, said there can never be a majority vote when there are two nominees for the trust and hence the resolution had to go for a casting vote.
"The decision (to reappoint Chandrasekaran) was taken after a unanimous vote. One of the directors (Noel Tata) holds the company hostage by saying he won't vote until things are done his way. It cannot be that if Noel Tata says no, it is a no. There could not have been a majority when there are only two directors," Mr. Salve contended.
Noel Tata says either it is his way or the highway, Mr. Salve argued and questioned as to why the suits were filed in November when the meeting and decision of reappointment were taken two months ago in September.
Mr. Salve added that the trusts, in their interim application, have not asked for deferment of the November 30 meeting. No prejudice would be caused if the meeting is held as scheduled. "The two trustees (SDTT and RDTT) cannot paralyse the company," he stated.
The suits said Article 121 of Tata Sons' AoA does not permit the chairman of a board meeting to exercise a casting vote in cases where the articles require the affirmative vote of a majority of the trustees.
The dispute follows Mr. Chandrasekaran's reappointment as Tata Sons executive chairman for five more years on September 17. The suits have claimed the Tata Sons board decision was "ultra vires the Articles of Association and is invalid, illegal, null and void".
Tata Trusts holds around 66% of Tata Sons and has sought a permanent order and injunction restraining the latter, its directors, officers and other agents from acting upon in any manner or giving effect to the resolution reappointing Mr. Chandrasekaran.

stories.headline: Bengaluru woman gives new Rs 12,540 silk saree for dry cleaning at Tumbledry, gets it back with burnt zari and black marks; consumer commission orders firm to pay full cost, Rs 10,000 compensation, Rs 5,000 litigation costs
stories.deck: A woman in Bengaluru faced a damaging experience when her new silk saree was returned in poor condition. She had entrusted three sarees to a Tumbledry outlet for dry cleaning, paying a fee of Rs 564. After discovering the damage, she sought help but received unsatisfactory responses. Eventually, she took legal action against the brand and its franchisee for their negligence.
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Imagine handing over a new silk saree, bought for a family occasion, to a dry cleaner, only to get it back with burnt zari and black marks. That is what a 51-year-old woman in Bengaluru faced after a routine cleaning at a Tumbledry outlet. The Bangalore (Urban) District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission has held the brand and its franchisee jointly and severally liable for deficiency in service and unfair trade practice.
The saga began when S Arathi, a resident of Wilson Garden, handed over three sarees for dry cleaning at the Tumbledry outlet in Basavangudi on September 1, 2024. She paid Rs 564, and delivery was fixed for September 4. On collecting them, she found one saree badly damaged. It was a new saree, bought on August 6, 2024 from Angadi Silks, Jayanagar, for Rs 12,540, and worn only for a few hours.
Arathi left the saree with the outlet, hoping for a quick resolution. Despite several visits from her home, she said she was ignored, promised calls that never came, or told that nothing could be done. She also said a blouse with handmade work, stitched at about Rs 5,000, could no longer be paired with any other saree.
She issued a legal notice on October 1, 2024. In its reply dated October 25, received on October 30, the outlet denied all allegations. It said the franchisee manager was contracted to handle grievances under the franchise agreement, and accused her of trying to extract undue benefit with a false narrative.
Frustrated, Arathi approached the commission on December 5, 2024, under Section 35 of the Consumer Protection Act, alleging deficiency in service. She sought Rs 12,540 for the saree and Rs 20,000 for mental agony and damages. She named the Tumbledry franchisee manager and Tumbledry, both at M/s Executive Laundry Building in Basavangudi.
Neither opposite party appeared or filed a version within the statutory period. They were placed ex-parte on April 1, 2025. The commission said the reply to the legal notice was only a pre-litigation reply and could not be treated as a version.
After going through the complainant's evidence, the commission observed that the invoice proved the sarees were entrusted for dry cleaning and that the photographs clearly showed burnt zari and black marks. It said the damage occurred while the saree was in the outlet's custody. The outlet produced no job card, process record or expert opinion to show the damage was pre-existing or due to a fabric defect, and mere denial in a notice reply was not evidence.
The commission held that a dry cleaner is a bailee under the Indian Contract Act and must take as much care of the goods as a prudent person would of their own. It said burning of zari during dry cleaning or ironing was a clear breach of that duty. It rejected the plea that only the franchisee was liable, saying the customer had dealt with an outlet displaying the Tumbledry name and that an internal franchise agreement cannot be used to defeat a consumer's claim.
The commission, comprising president Ramachandra M S and members Nandini H Kumbhar and Savitha Airani, allowed the complaint in part on November 21. It directed the opposite parties, jointly and severally, to pay Rs 12,540 for the saree, refund Rs 564 in dry cleaning charges, and pay Rs 10,000 as compensation and Rs 5000 as litigation costs.

stories.headline: 70-year-old Karnataka woman gifts property to daughter-in-law, approaches tribunal to reclaim it after 22 years; Karnataka HC says Senior Citizens Act cannot undo old transfer but retains Rs 4,000 monthly maintenance order
stories.deck: The Karnataka High Court recently overturned a tribunal's decision to cancel a 2000 property gift deed. The elderly woman claimed that her daughter-in-law obtained the deed through fraud, but the court found otherwise. The gift deed was registered and the transfer was legally completed prior to the relevant law's enactment. The sister-in-law will continue payments of Rs 4,000 each month to her…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: A gift made in 2000 cannot be undone using a law that came into force eight years later, the Karnataka High Court has ruled, overturning a tribunal's decision to cancel a 70-year-old woman's transfer of property to her daughter-in-law. The court, however, retained the latter's obligation to pay the elderly woman Rs 4,000 every month for the rest of her life.
The dispute arose from a registered gift deed dated July 29, 2000, through which the woman transferred her properties to her daughter-in-law and handed over possession. The deed stated that the transfer was made out of love and affection and to protect the properties, as the woman's son was habituated to certain vices.
The arrangement remained in place for nearly 22 years before the elderly woman approached the Senior Citizens Maintenance Tribunal, seeking to get the transfer reversed. She accused her daughter-in-law of securing the deed through fraud and misrepresentation.
The tribunal first rejected her plea on January 5, 2023, saying that a dispute over cancellation of a gift deed had to be dealt with by a civil court. But it subsequently passed another order on July 3, 2023, cancelling the deed and directing revenue officials to alter the property records. 
This was done without issuing notice to the daughter-in-law.
Challenging the decision, the daughter-in-law told the high court that the transfer had taken place in 2000, whereas the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act came into force only on April 1, 2008. She argued that the provisions of the Act could not be used to set aside a transaction completed before the legislation existed.
The high court found merit in the argument. It pointed out that the gift deed was registered and that the elderly woman had waited almost 22 years before approaching the tribunal. The court said the 2007 Act was prospective in nature and could not be used to invalidate property transfers made before April 1, 2008. It held that the tribunal had no jurisdiction to cancel the registered deed and quashed its decision to interfere with the property transfer.
The daughter-in-law had, however, expressed her willingness to continue paying Rs 4,000 a month to her mother-in-law despite challenging the tribunal's order. The court allowed the maintenance direction to remain in force, meaning the daughter-in-law will have to pay the elderly woman Rs 4,000 every month throughout her lifetime.

stories.headline: Karnataka government serves show-cause notice to IOCL terminal in Bengaluru over ethanol measurement discrepancies
stories.deck: The action follows inspections initiated by the Department of Legal Metrology, Karnataka, at the terminals of oil marketing companies, taking the checks of fuel samples for ethanol blend one step further
stories.bodyText:
The Karnataka government on Friday served a show-cause notice on Indian Oil Corporation Limited (IOCL) over discrepancies in the measurement of ethanol and motor gasoline at its terminal in Devanagonthi, Bengaluru, and directed the oil marketing company (OMC) to submit an explanation within seven days.
The action follows inspections initiated by the Department of Legal Metrology, Karnataka, at the terminals of oil marketing companies.
Tests of samples from petrol stations in Karnataka by the State government had revealed ethanol blending to be as high as 32% in some cases, Food, Civil Supplies, Consumer Affairs and Legal Metrology Minister Rizwan Arshad claimed earlier this month. This was denied by OMCs and Union Ministers.
Mr. Arshad had also written to the Union government seeking display of accurate ethanol blending in petrol at every station.
Show-cause notice
According to the show-cause notice, officials detected discrepancies in the quantities of ethanol and motor gasoline dispensed through mass flow meters during an inspection at the IOCL terminal on Wednesday (November 25).
According to the Minister, the inspection was conducted using the “master proving” test method. At Bay No. 9, officials found that the meter was dispensing 14 litres of ethanol in excess for every 3,000 litres. At the same bay, the quantity of motor gasoline supplied was found to be 4 to 6 litres short for every 3,000 litres. Another mass flow meter at Bay No. 4 was also found to be dispensing an additional three litres of ethanol for every 3,000 litres, the notice stated.
Mr. Arshad said that the discrepancies exceeded the permissible limits prescribed under the Legal Metrology Act, 2009, and the rules framed under it. “The inaccuracies in measurement could adversely affect the interests of consumers, distributors and other stakeholders dealing with petroleum products,” he said.
The show-cause notice, issued to the Deputy General Manager in charge of the Devanagonthi terminal, has sought a written explanation within seven days of its receipt, warning that failure to submit a satisfactory explanation within the stipulated period could lead to further legal and departmental action against the terminal and the officials responsible.
The department has asked IOCL to explain the reasons behind the discrepancies and provide details of the measures taken to ensure the accuracy of the mass flow meters and associated batch control units. It has also sought records of their latest calibration and maintenance, along with details of corrective measures proposed to address the discrepancies.
Further, the department has directed IOCL not to use the affected measurement systems for commercial transactions until their accuracy and compliance with prescribed legal standards are verified.

stories.headline: Boyfriend stabs Kerala nursing graduate to death in Bengaluru lodge after argument
stories.bodyText:
A 22-year-old nursing graduate from Kerala was allegedly stabbed to death by her boyfriend at a lodge in Bengaluru’s Cottonpete area on Friday morning following an argument. The Cottonpete police have arrested the accused and are questioning him to ascertain the motive behind the murder.
The deceased has been identified as Ganga, a native of Adoor in Kerala. She had completed her nursing course and had come to Bengaluru in search of a job.
The accused, Gokul Krishna, 23, hails from Kollam district in Kerala. He had completed BSc Nursing and was working as a consultant helping nursing aspirants secure college admissions. He had accompanied her to Bengaluru and the two had been in a relationship for the past four years, police said.
According to preliminary investigations, the couple arrived in Bengaluru from Kerala on Thursday and checked into Regency Lodge on OTC Road, near Thawakkal Mastan Dargah, on November 26. Around 11 am on Friday, the two allegedly got into an argument, following which Gokul attacked Ganga with a knife and stabbed her in the abdomen.
Following the incident, the accused allegedly informed the lodge management, who alerted the police. Ganga was rushed to a nearby hospital but succumbed to her injuries.
The Cottonpete police, along with the dog squad and Forensic Science Laboratory (FSL) personnel, visited the lodge and conducted an investigation.
A murder case has been registered at the Cottonpete police station under the provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS). “We are questioning the accused to ascertain the exact motive behind the attack. We are also investigating where and how he procured the knife,” a senior police officer said.
Further investigation is under way.

briefs.headline: Relocation drive under lens as elephants return to Karnataka's Belur
briefs.deck: A herd of elephants was relocated from Belur in Hassan to Mudigere in Chikkamagaluru because of local conflicts. Despite the forest department's efforts, around 20 elephants returned to Belur shortly after the relocation process. Residents and coffee growers are concerned about potential damage to their plantations from the elephants, causing fear among agricultural workers. The Belur MLA…
briefs.bodyText:
By: KG Suresh
HASSAN: With the govt and forest dept seemingly lacking a clear plan to relocate them, a herd of elephants, including six calves, has been forced to trek nearly 20km between Hassan and Chikkamagaluru districts. Half the jumbos are back where the relocation exercise began, raising questions about the efficacy of the entire operation.
Three days after 40 elephants were driven out of Belur in Hassan and into Mudigere in Chikkamagaluru, about 20 of them were back in Belur Friday. The rest are also likely to return to the same area soon. Though officials have remained tight-lipped about why these elephants moved back, sources claimed the reversal was due to opposition from residents and legislators in Chikkamagaluru.
With residents and coffee growers, on edge that the herd could damage their plantations and property, they pushed the elephants back towards Hassan, sources said.
The relocation operation, involving forest officials, staff and trained elephants, cost lakhs. The return of half the herd has effectively undone much of that effort.
Foresters in Hassan confirmed that the elephants were camping near Aramane Gudda, Puttammana Kadu, Mallapura and Kanahalli. 
The department has deployed over 100 personnel to monitor their movements and ensure the safety of residents.
The herd, initially spread across six groups, was driven out of Belur starting Nov 20. Over the next three days, forest department personnel, assisted by trained elephants, pushed the jumbos towards the forested areas in Mudigere. By Nov 23, all 40 had been moved into Chikkamagaluru district. Harish Gowda, a farmer and former gram panchayat president, said the forest department had moved the elephants to Chikkamagaluru to address the problem in Belur, but a section of the herd returned.
With coffee harvesting under way, agricultural workers are afraid to enter plantations in Nagenahalli, Kogodu and neighbouring areas. Even those reporting for work are doing so under constant fear of elephant attacks.
Belur MLA HK Suresh strongly condemned the relocation exercise and gave the govt and district in-charge minister KM Shivalinge Gowda a one-day deadline starting Friday to resolve the issue.
A meeting with coffee growers and farmers is planned, while a meeting of ministers and MLAs under the chief minister's leadership is scheduled for Nov 30.
Farmers have demanded a permanent solution to the recurring elephant menace.

briefs.headline: Ticketless travel: Karnataka high court upholds reinstatement of dismissed bus conductor, cites denial of fair hearing
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The high court has upheld an order directing North Western Karnataka Road Transport Corporation (NWKRTC) to reinstate a conductor dismissed for failing to issue tickets to two passengers, holding that an employee’s right to explain cannot be denied on the assumption that it wouldn’t affect the outcome.
A division bench of Justices M Nagaprasanna and Hema Kulkarni dismissed NWKRTC’s writ appeal against the Nov 10, 2022, single-bench order in favour of conductor Mantayya. The bench said prejudice was measured not by the certainty of a different result, but by denial of the meaningful opportunity the law intended an employee to have before the decision.
A checking squad intercepted Mantayya’s bus in Aug 2012 and found that he had neither issued tickets to two passengers nor collected the fare of Rs 146 per ticket. Following disciplinary proceedings, he was dismissed in 2014. A labour court rejected his plea in 2016, prompting him to approach the high court.
The single bench found non-compliance with regulation 23(18) of KSRTC Servants (Conduct and Discipline) Regulations, 1971, which requires an opportunity for a delinquent employee to explain his position. It ordered reinstatement and modified the dismissal to withholding two increments with cumulative effect.
NWKRTC argued that Mantayya could not invoke the regulation after participating in the inquiry. However, the division bench noted that he had not examined himself and was denied time to present defence evidence after management’s evidence closed. The mandatory questioning under regulation 23(18) was also not conducted before the finding of guilt and dismissal.
The bench said the prejudice was evident because Mantayya had been denied both the opportunity to lead defence evidence and the final statutory chance to explain the incriminating circumstances. It said an inquiry officer must ensure fairness and the authority to punish remained subordinate to the obligation to act fairly.

briefs.headline: Bank guarantee isn’t furnished for it to be photo-framed & hung on wall, says Karnataka high court in forfeiture case
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Karnataka high court has dismissed a writ appeal by the city-based Travel World against Hubli Electricity Supply Company’s forfeiture of two bank guarantees worth Rs 36.7 lakh and Rs 36.4 lakh.
A division bench of Justices M Nagaprasanna and Hema Kulkarni observed that a bank guarantee was not furnished to be photo-framed and hung on a wall, but to be executed at the relevant time.
In 2022, Hescom issued Travel World a letter of intent and a work order to provide vehicles for officers’ commutation and transportation of transformers in its Belagavi and Hubballi zones on a rate-contract basis.
The services were later stopped unilaterally and did not resume despite notices. Hescom forfeited the two guarantees in 2025. A single bench dismissed Travel World’s petition challenging the forfeiture on Aug 1, 2025, prompting the appeal to the division bench.
Travel World argued that Hescom could not directly invoke the forfeiture clause without determining the loss caused by the alleged failure to provide adequate services. It contended that withdrawal of services should not automatically result in contract termination or complete forfeiture of the guarantees.
Hescom, on the other hand, argued that the sudden stoppage and withdrawal of services warranted forfeiture under the contract.
The bench noted that the Supreme Court, in the Hindustan Steels Ltd vs Tarapore & Company case, had held that invocation of a bank guarantee was a natural corollary when a contract was breached.
It also cited UP Co-operative Federation vs Singh Consultants and Engineers Pvt Ltd, in which the apex court opposed high court intervention in execution or encashment of bank guarantees except in specified circumstances.
“We, therefore, don’t find any error in the order of the single bench for us to interfere in this intra-court appeal,” the HC bench ruled.

briefs.headline: Water woes: Bengaluru’s dhobi ghats turn to tankers, restrict washing to alternate days
briefs.deck: As borewells in most of the dhobi ghats in the city run dry, washermen turn to water tankers; due to less water availability, many families have given up the job limiting themselves to ironing clothes
briefs.bodyText:
For washermen working in dhobi ghats in various parts of the city, water is no longer an easy source to secure but a scarce commodity especially during the ongoing drought. As borewells in most of the dhobi ghats have run dry, dhobis either depend on water from traditional wells and sometimes even water tankers. To handle the crisis, washermen have decided to wash clothes only alternate days.
Challenge
There are around 31 dhobi ghats in the city which are over 100 years old. According to the members of washermen community, they need 25,000 to 1,00,000 litres of water depending on the number of clothes to wash every day. However, meeting this substantial demand becomes a major challenge during drought and inadequate rains as borewells run dry and water level in traditional wells also reduce.
For instance, the dhobi ghat located in Rajajinagar is heavily dependent on tanker water every day.
Gangaraju, secretary, Bengaluru North Madiwala Mahajana Sangha, said, “Since there is no traditional well or lakes nearby, we had drilled borewells. Out of 17 borewells, one was working but it has failed due to a lack of rains. We go for 10 tankers every day which costs ₹800 per tanker. Around 60,000 litres of water are required to wash clothes on a daily basis. The demand increases during summer and dhobis go for 15 to 20 tankers a day.”
Muniraju, president, Anjanapura Madiwalara Kshemabhivruddi Sangha, said that on an average they require 25,000 litres of water every day. “If all the 65 people wash clothes, we need 50,000 litres every day but because of shortage of water, they wash in batches on alternate days limiting it to 25,000 litres per day,” he said, adding, “One out of six borewells is currently functioning.”
He stressed that due to less water availability, other families have taken up washing activity on a private basis by installing washing machines at their individual house and few have limited themselves to ironing clothes.
The picture is no different in Ulsoor Lake dhobi ghat as washermen depend on water from a traditional well close to the lake.
Hari Kishan, president, Ulsoor Dhobi Ghat Madiwalara Sangha, said, “We had drilled one borewell but it doesn’t function in the absence of rains and drought conditions. We have a traditional well from where water is drawn using electric motor and clothes are washed. The level of water in well depends on the level of water in the lake, this year, the water in well has decreased. At present, there are less than 80 families that use the facility here to wash and dry clothes.”
Despite mounting water woes in dhobi ghats in the city, the members of washermen community are striving to retain their roots and the land allocated specially to carry out their occupation.

briefs.headline: Harbhajan Singh gets a garland, a toss and a taste of gully cricket in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Harbhajan Singh
 is all for cricket, no matter how it’s played. So, when he landed in Bengaluru to kick off the Indian Softball Cricket League (ISCL), that is also being supported by 
Bangalore Times
, the ace spinner was excited about the idea of a faster, more action-packed version of the game.
“I will always support cricket in any form. The fast-paced format excites me. The concept of Gully to Glory is quite intriguing, and I’m glad to be a part of it. I relate to the concept and hope to see many players go on to represent the country,” he said.
I will always support cricket in any form. The fast-paced format excites me. The concept of Gully to Glory is quite intriguing, and I’m glad to be a part of it. I relate to the concept and hope to see many players go on to represent the country
Harbhajan Singh
But the welcome he received in Bengaluru had a surprise of its own. A giant garland was brought out for the cricketer, leaving him visibly amused. “I’ve never seen a garland this big, nor did I expect one for myself. I’ve seen visuals of our PM Narendra Modi being welcomed in Bengaluru with a huge garland, but I never thought I’d get one,” he said, before turning to the photographers with a request: “
Mujhe ye haar wala photo chahiye!
 (I want the pictures of me with the garland!)”

briefs.headline: Delimitation: 50% hike in seats could see Karnataka’s share unchanged in the Lok Sabha, but a similar change at assembly level would produce drastic churn
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: With the Union cabinet reportedly clearing a fresh delimitation-linked women’s reservation bill, the special sitting of Parliament from Monday could reopen a politically sensitive question for 
Karnataka
: will delimitation alter the representation in Parliament and assembly?
The stakes go beyond a bigger House. Constituency boundaries, regional clout and the balance between 
BJP
, 
Congress
 and JD(S) could shift. The Centre’s stated calculation in April of a 50% increase in seats offers one way to gauge the impact — even if that version of the bill was defeated. 
This may be the most visible change for voters. With 33% reservation, about 112 seats in a 336-member assembly would be reserved for women, along with 14 of the 42 Lok Sabha seats. Only 10 women were elected in the 2023 assembly polls, so the reserved pool alone would be more than 11 times that number. “This could significantly change the political landscape,” said Vishwas Shetty, a political commentator. “Reservation would open a much larger pool of opportunities for women, and rotation of reserved seats would affect sitting legislators and candidate selection.”

briefs.headline: Improve girls’ schools in Karnataka, adopt long-term CSR projects: Governor
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: Governor Sudha Yadhav on Friday urged industry leaders to improve girls’ schools in 
Karnataka
’s villages and adopt long-term CSR projects in remote areas.
“Can we improve the condition of girls’ schools in all the villages of Karnataka?” she asked at the BCIC CSR Conclave and Awards Ceremony 2026, organised by Bangalore Chamber of Industry and Commerce, the state’s industry apex body.
Yadhav said toilets were still absent in rural schools and hostels attended by girls. Industries planted lakhs of saplings but failed to maintain them, with only about 10% surviving, she said.
Recalling a visit to a tribal village in Chitradurga, she said four villages had only one graduate, while school infrastructure was poor and people walked barefoot.
She urged firms not to shift funds between causes each year, but to select one project, prepare a roadmap and work in far-flung areas. She asked the chamber to present an analysis next year of the progress achieved and work remaining.
As part of its 50th-year celebrations, BCIC announced three CSR initiatives. Cancer awareness programmes will cover about 4,000 students at 10 schools and 10 colleges, while breast cancer screening will cover at least 500 underprivileged beneficiaries.
A Ward Impact Lab will bring together architects, planners and residents to design small-scale, ward-level projects eligible for CSR funding. 
BCIC will also plant 10,000 saplings across Bengaluru and Mysuru over the next year.
BCIC president K Ravi said: “By focusing on these critical areas, we move beyond mere philanthropy to create lasting grassroots impact. Women’s employment unlocks half of our demographic dividend, and ethical governance keeps progress transparent.”
Winners of BCIC awards 2026
Education - Sansera Engineering Ltd and Bangalore International Airport Ltd jointly won in the corporate category, while Akshara and TIE Foundation shared the non-profit award
Healthcare - Biocon Foundation won the corporate award, while Indian Cancer Society and Centre for Cellular and Molecular Platforms (C-CAMP) shared the non-profit award
Corporate environment - Tamara Leisure Experiences Pvt Ltd won and Sahyadri Community Development and Women Empowerment Society (SCODWES) was recognised in the non-profit category.
The Karur Vysya Bank Ltd won the corporate award for skilling and livelihood, while TVS Srinivasan Services Trust received the corporate award for women empowerment.
